clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in NLRC4, producing a constitutively over-active NLRC4 inflammasome.
Distinctive for recurrent macrophage activation syndrome / haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis together with severe, often neonatal-onset enterocolitis.
Markedly elevated interleukin-18 is a hallmark biomarker, typically far higher than in other autoinflammatory diseases.
Excess caspase-1 activation drives both interleukin-1beta and, especially, free interleukin-18, which fuels macrophage activation.
Some NLRC4 mutations instead produce a milder cold-induced urticarial phenotype (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome type 4).
Flares may be life-threatening, with fever, cytopenias, hyperferritinaemia, coagulopathy and secretory diarrhoea.

Interleukin-1 blockade, interleukin-18 blockade with recombinant interleukin-18 binding protein, and interferon-gamma neutralisation are used; interleukin-1 inhibition alone may be insufficient given the dominant interleukin-18 and interferon-gamma drive.
reference.pathophysiology: NLRC4 (NLR family CARD domain-containing protein 4) is a cytosolic pattern-recognition receptor that, on sensing bacterial flagellin and type III secretion system components via NAIP proteins, oligomerises to form an inflammasome that activates caspase-1. Germline heterozygous gain-of-function mutations, typically within the nucleotide-binding domain, lower the activation threshold or lock NLRC4 in an active conformation, causing spontaneous, ligand-independent inflammasome assembly. The resulting unrestrained caspase-1 activity generates large amounts of interleukin-1beta and, characteristically, interleukin-18, along with pyroptotic cell death; the extreme interleukin-18 excess promotes interferon-gamma-driven macrophage activation and haemophagocytosis. Overactivation of the inflammasome in intestinal epithelium and myeloid cells underlies the severe infantile enterocolitis, while systemic cytokine release produces recurrent macrophage activation syndrome; certain mutations instead confer a cold-induced urticarial phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Familial or primary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (perforin-pathway and degranulation defects)
Secondary macrophage activation syndrome complicating systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or infection
Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (NLRP3) and other inflammasomopathies
Very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease and monogenic enteropathies such as IL-10 or IL-10 receptor defects
Other interleukin-18-high autoinflammatory disorders such as XIAP deficiency and CDC42-related NOCARH syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Sequencing of NLRC4 within a haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis / autoinflammatory gene panel, with attention to somatic mosaicism
Serum interleukin-18, characteristically very high, with interleukin-18 and CXCL9 profiling
Ferritin and other macrophage-activation markers trended qualitatively across flares
Full blood count for cytopenias, together with coagulation and triglyceride assessment interpreted qualitatively
Bone marrow examination for haemophagocytosis when macrophage activation is suspected
Endoscopy and intestinal biopsy in infantile enterocolitis
Functional inflammasome and caspase-1 activation assays where available
redFlags: Neonatal or early-infantile severe secretory diarrhoea and enterocolitis with failure to thrive
Recurrent episodes of fever with cytopenias, hyperferritinaemia and coagulopathy indicating macrophage activation
Family history of infantile enterocolitis or unexplained macrophage activation syndrome
reference.prognosis: The severe enterocolitis-plus-macrophage-activation phenotype can be fatal in infancy without prompt cytokine-directed therapy, though outcomes have improved with interleukin-1, interleukin-18 and interferon-gamma-targeted treatments; the milder cold-urticarial variants have a relatively good prognosis.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent macrophage activation as secondary to infection or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and missing the monogenic cause.
Relying on interleukin-1 blockade alone, which may fail because of the dominant interleukin-18 and interferon-gamma signalling.
Overlooking somatic mosaicism, which can cause disease despite a normal-appearing germline result.
Mistaking the neonatal enterocolitis for infectious or allergic colitis.
Under-recognising interleukin-18 as the key discriminating biomarker.
references: International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) inborn errors of immunity classification
Textbook of autoinflammatory diseases and paediatric rheumatology references
management: Use interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra as the cornerstone of cytokine-directed therapy
Add interleukin-18-targeted therapy with recombinant interleukin-18 binding protein (tadekinig alfa) given the characteristic extreme interleukin-18 excess
Treat macrophage activation syndrome and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis flares with corticosteroids and interferon-gamma neutralisation (emapalumab), alongside intensive supportive care
Manage the neonatal enterocolitis with fluid and electrolyte correction and parenteral nutrition during severe secretory diarrhoea
Monitor for impending macrophage activation with serial ferritin, blood counts, coagulation and interleukin-18 trends
Coordinate care through clinical immunology and rheumatology with intensive care involvement for crises
Offer genetic counselling and family evaluation, noting heterozygous gain-of-function inheritance and possible somatic mosaicism
